Model comparison

We compared the hierarchical model with parametric alternatives across all experimental batches12,15. Posterior predictive checks were computed for every strain, and the expected log predictive density was estimated with leave-one-out cross validation [34]. The hierarchical model consistently improved predictive accuracy when batch effects were present, while performing similarly to simpler models in their absence.

Table 1 summarises the comparison. Differences were largest for strains grown under oxidative stress, where parametric growth curves failed to capture the delayed recovery phase observed in the data.

Hierarchical models for growth curve analysis

A. Researcher and B. Scientist

1. Introduction

Microbial growth curves are routinely measured in high throughput plate readers. These measurements are affected by many sources of variation, including differences between batches, plates and wells. Traditional analyses summarise each curve with a small number of parameters and ignore this structure, which can lead to biased estimates and overconfident conclusions.

In this work we develop a hierarchical model that represents each level of variation explicitly. The model provides estimates of biological effects together with their uncertainty and allows researchers to quantify the relative importance of technical factors.1

2. Methods

Growth was measured every thirty minutes for forty eight hours. Each experiment included at least three biological replicates and three technical replicates per condition. Optical density was log transformed and normalised to the first measurement of each well before analysis.

Model parameters were estimated with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo using four chains of two thousand iterations each. Convergence was assessed with the potential scale reduction factor, and all parameters satisfied the conventional threshold.

3. Results

The hierarchical model identified strong batch effects in two of the five experiments. After accounting for these effects, the estimated difference between treatment and control growth rates decreased by approximately thirty percent, and the corresponding credible intervals became wider but better calibrated.

Simulation studies confirmed that ignoring batch structure inflates the false discovery rate when the number of replicates is small. The proposed approach maintained nominal error rates across all simulated scenarios.

Bayesian inference. The unknown functions (mðtÞ; dðtÞ; apðtÞ; bcðtÞ; and ðabÞp;cðtÞ), kernel hyperparameters (s2 l and ‘l) for each group of latent functions, and observation noise parameters (s2 y) are all estimated by Bayesian statistical inference. In Bayesian inference, prior distributions on unknown quantities (e.g. pðmðtÞ; ymÞ ¼ pðmðtÞjymÞ × pðymÞ) are combined with the likelihood, pðyðtÞjmðtÞÞ to obtain the posterior distribution pðmðtÞ; ymjyðtÞÞ.

Latent functions are grouped by shared kernel hyperparameters yl ¼ fs2 l; ‘lg into related sets (e.g. treatment effects, interaction effects, batch effects), which then provide the GP prior for the latent function. For each group, s2 l is assigned a Gammaða; bÞ prior, with fixed effects assigned as a Gammað10; 10Þ prior and random effects assigned a Gammað7; 10Þ prior. ‘l was assigned an inverse- Gammaða; bÞ prior, with parameter a ¼ 6 and b ¼ 1 for H. salinarum, and a ¼ 2, b ¼ 3 for P. aeruginosa fixed effects and a ¼ 10, b ¼ 1 for P. aeruginosa random effects. Noise variance s2 y was also assigned a gamma prior.

Bayesian inference was then performed, with the posterior distribution obtained by sampling using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) implemented with the Stan library, which uses a Hamiltonian Monte-Carlo procedure with No-U-turn sampling [55]. Multiple chains were run to diagnose convergence, with all parameter posterior means confirmed to have con-
verged within R^ < 1:1 as recommended [56].

Results

In the dataset used here, population growth for each of P. aeruginosa and H. salinarum cultures was monitored under standard (non-stressed) conditions vs. stress conditions (see Materials and methods and references [22, 23] for precise definition of standard conditions).
